questions.learningObjective: Identify which region of a sentence produces longer fixation durations
questions.stem: A software team's ticket asks which sentence region shows longer eye fixations when a garden-path parse is forced; the trace shows the verb phrase

options.text: The disambiguating word after the ambiguity is fixated longest
The first noun phrase is fixated longest because it anchors the whole parse
options.misconception: confuses initial anchoring with reanalysis cost

options.text: The final punctuation mark draws the longest fixation on every trial
options.misconception: treats line-end scanning as structural processing

options.text: The sentence-initial capital letter produces the longest fixation
options.misconception: confuses orthographic salience with syntactic load

questions.explanation: Reanalysis after a garden-path misparse lands on the disambiguating word, producing the longest fixation there. Initial nouns and punctuation are not the locus of structural repair.
questions.hint: Look for the word that forces the parse to change

questions.stem: A software team's ticket reports that group X judges related word pairs faster than group Y, but only when the pairs share a category

options.text: The groups differ in low-level visual speed rather than meaning access
options.misconception: attributes a semantic effect to peripheral speed

options.text: Group Y lacks any semantic knowledge of the tested words
options.misconception: overstates a relative slowdown as absence

options.text: Group X has stronger semantic networks for category relations
The rhyme advantage proves group Y is overall faster at language
options.misconception: generalises a narrow advantage to overall speed

questions.explanation: A category-specific advantage that survives vocabulary matching points to stronger semantic networks for category relations in group X. The rhyme advantage is a separate, narrow effect.
questions.hint: Match the advantage to its specific condition

questions.topic: Language: A Sentence That Is Slow Because of One Structural Choice
questions.learningObjective: Explain why one structural choice slows sentence processing
questions.stem: A software team's ticket describes a sentence that is slow because it places a long modifier between a subject and its verb

answer.exemplar: The long modifier interrupts the dependency between subject and verb, forcing the parser to hold the subject in memory while the modifier is processed, which increases working-memory load and slows reading before the verb arrives

questions.explanation: Inserting a long modifier between subject and verb forces the parser to retain the subject across the modifier, increasing working-memory load and slowing processing until the verb resolves the dependency.
questions.hint: Focus on the memory cost of holding the subject

questions.learningObjective: Compute the predicted slowdown from word frequency and predictability
questions.stem: A software team's ticket gives a rare word with base reading time 400 ms and a predictability reduction of 120 ms; what is the predicted reading time
questions.explanation: Predicted reading time equals base time minus the predictability reduction: 400 minus 120 equals 280 ms. The rare word remains slow but predictability offsets part of the cost.
questions.hint: Subtract the predictability reduction from base time

questions.stem: A software team's ticket asks how a centre-embedded relative clause slows reading and what memory account explains it

answer.exemplar: Centre embedding nests a clause inside the subject-verb dependency, forcing the reader to retain the outer subject while parsing the inner clause; limited working memory makes the nested dependency costly, so reading slows at the embedded clause and recovers after it

questions.learningObjective: Design a comprehension assessment for fluent aphasia
questions.stem: A software team's ticket asks for a design assessing comprehension in a patient with fluent but meaningless speech

answer.exemplar: Use picture-pointing and yes-no comprehension tasks matched to the patient's fluent output level, include semantic and syntactic contrasts, and compare performance to age-matched controls

questions.explanation: Picture-pointing and yes-no tasks matched to output level, with semantic and syntactic contrasts and control comparison, assess comprehension independently of production. This isolates the comprehension deficit.
questions.hint: Test comprehension without requiring speech

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: A Failure of Repetition That Locates the Problem
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise repetition failure into a disconnection account
questions.stem: A software team's ticket synthesises a case of intact comprehension and production with failed repetition; propose the mechanism

answer.exemplar: Repetition requires transferring a heard form from comprehension to production; when the connecting tract is damaged, the form cannot reach production even though both endpoints work, so repetition fails selectively

questions.explanation: Repetition requires transferring a heard form from comprehension to production. When the connecting tract is damaged, the form cannot reach production even though both endpoints work, so repetition fails selectively.
questions.hint: Repetition needs the link between the two areas

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: A Word That Cannot Be Found but Is Clearly Known
questions.learningObjective: Identify which cue best resolves a TOT state
questions.stem: A software team's ticket asks which cue most often resolves a tip-of-the-tongue state

options.text: A semantic category cue such as 'it is an animal'
A definition repeating the meaning already known
A first-letter cue providing the initial phoneme
A visual picture of the referent

questions.explanation: A first-letter cue providing the initial phoneme most often resolves TOT states because it supplies the missing phonological information. Semantic and visual cues do not directly fill the phonological gap.
questions.hint: The gap is phonological, so phonological cues help

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Where the Difficulty of a Sentence Lands in the Eye Record
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a region-of-interest fixation comparison

stimulus.body: A ticketed eye-tracking study compares garden-path and control sentences: fixation time on the disambiguating word is 280 ms in garden-path sentences versus 160 ms in controls, while earlier regions do not differ.

questions.stem: A software team's ticket shows 280 ms versus 160 ms fixations on the disambiguating word

options.text: The difference reflects initial lexical access cost
options.misconception: attributes reanalysis cost to first access

options.text: The difference shows readers skip the disambiguating word
The difference is due to longer words in the garden-path condition
The difference reflects reanalysis at the disambiguating word

questions.explanation: A 120 ms difference localized to the disambiguating word, with earlier regions matched, reflects reanalysis at that word. Lexical access, length, and skipping accounts are ruled out by the design.
questions.hint: Localised cost at the revision point

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Two Groups Judging Word Meaning, and What the Difference Shows
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a category-specific group difference indicates
questions.stem: A software team's ticket asks what a category-specific speed advantage in one group indicates

options.text: Stronger semantic networks for category relations
A general processing speed advantage across all tasks
Better visual acuity for written words
options.misconception: attributes a semantic effect to vision

options.text: Larger vocabulary size in the faster group

questions.explanation: A category-specific advantage indicates stronger semantic networks for category relations, not a general speed, visual, or vocabulary advantage. The specificity rules out those alternatives.
questions.hint: Specificity points to category networks

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: A Sentence That Is Slow Because of One Structural Choice
questions.learningObjective: Compute the reading-time cost of a structural choice
questions.stem: A software team's ticket gives reading time 540 ms with a long modifier and 360 ms without; what is the cost
questions.explanation: The cost is 540 minus 360, which equals 180 ms. The long modifier between subject and verb adds that processing cost.
questions.hint: Subtract the no-modifier time from the modifier time

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Why a Rare Word Is Slow Even When It Is Predictable
questions.learningObjective: Design a study of frequency and predictability in reading
questions.stem: A software team's ticket asks for a design testing whether predictability eliminates frequency effects

answer.exemplar: Cross frequency and predictability in a 2x2 design, measure fixation durations, and test the interaction; a significant interaction would show predictability does not fully eliminate frequency effects

questions.explanation: A 2x2 design crossing frequency and predictability, with fixation durations and an interaction test, directly addresses whether predictability eliminates frequency effects. A significant interaction would refute full elimination.
questions.hint: Test the interaction, not just main effects

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: A Picture That Has Been Named Before It Is Shown
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise priming findings into a lexical activation account
questions.stem: A software team's ticket synthesises a 90 ms naming benefit after a spoken name prime; propose the mechanism

answer.exemplar: The spoken name pre-activates the lexical entry for that concept, so when the picture appears the entry is already partially activated and naming completes faster by about 90 ms

questions.explanation: A spoken-name prime pre-activates the lexical entry for that concept, so naming the picture completes faster by about 90 ms. The benefit is localized to the primed concept.
questions.hint: Pre-activation of the lexical entry speeds naming

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Two Word Kinds, Two Interference Effects
questions.learningObjective: Identify which word kind produces which interference
questions.stem: A software team's ticket asks which word kind produces semantic interference in naming

options.text: Phonologically related distractors produce semantic interference
Unrelated distractors produce the strongest interference
Semantically related distractors produce semantic interference
High-frequency distractors always produce semantic interference

questions.explanation: Semantically related distractors produce semantic interference in naming. Phonological overlap produces facilitation, not semantic interference, and unrelated distractors do not interfere strongly.
questions.hint: Match the distractor type to the interference type

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: A Damaged Area and the Loss It Produces
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a lesion-language profile in a case study

stimulus.body: A ticketed case shows a patient with left temporal damage who speaks fluently but cannot comprehend spoken sentences and repeats poorly. Naming is also impaired.

questions.stem: A software team's ticket shows left temporal damage with fluent speech but poor comprehension

options.text: The profile indicates frontal damage with production deficit
options.misconception: mislocalises temporal damage to frontal cortex

options.text: The profile indicates motor speech disorder without language loss
The profile indicates a pure disconnection syndrome
options.misconception: overstates the repetition deficit as pure disconnection

options.text: The profile indicates Wernicke's aphasia from temporal damage

questions.explanation: Left temporal damage with fluent speech and poor comprehension is Wernicke's aphasia. Frontal damage would impair production, and a pure disconnection would spare comprehension.
questions.hint: Temporal damage plus fluent poor comprehension is Wernicke's

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Speech That Flows but Cannot Be Checked Against Its Meaning
questions.learningObjective: Compute the comprehension score in a fluent aphasia case
questions.stem: A software team's ticket gives 18 correct out of 30 comprehension items for a fluent aphasia patient; what is the accuracy
questions.explanation: Accuracy is 18 divided by 30, which equals 0.6. The patient answers 60 percent of comprehension items correctly despite fluent output.
questions.hint: Divide correct by total items

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: A Failure of Repetition That Locates the Problem
questions.learningObjective: Design a repetition task battery for disconnection cases
questions.stem: A software team's ticket asks for a design testing whether repetition failure is due to disconnection

answer.exemplar: Test repetition of words and nonwords, compare to comprehension and production baselines, and include a white-matter imaging measure to link tract integrity to repetition accuracy

questions.explanation: Testing repetition of words and nonwords against comprehension and production baselines, with white-matter imaging, links tract integrity to repetition accuracy and confirms a disconnection account.
questions.hint: Compare repetition to both endpoints and image the tract

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: A Word That Cannot Be Found but Is Clearly Known
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise TOT findings into a partial-activation account
questions.stem: A software team's ticket synthesises TOT states where meaning is known but sound is missing; propose the mechanism

answer.exemplar: The tip-of-the-tongue state arises when semantic activation is strong enough to create a feeling of knowing, but phonological activation is incomplete, so the word's sound form cannot be fully specified for articulation

questions.explanation: TOT states arise when semantic activation creates a feeling of knowing but phonological activation is incomplete, so the sound form cannot be fully specified for articulation. The dissociation is between meaning and sound retrieval.
questions.hint: Meaning is retrieved but sound is not

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Where the Difficulty of a Sentence Lands in the Eye Record
questions.learningObjective: Identify the reanalysis locus in a garden-path sentence
questions.stem: A software team's ticket asks where reanalysis cost appears in a garden-path sentence

options.text: At the disambiguating word after the ambiguity
At the sentence-initial subject noun
options.misconception: attributes reanalysis to the first phrase

options.text: At the final punctuation of the sentence
options.misconception: treats line end as the revision point

options.text: Uniformly across all words of the sentence

questions.explanation: Reanalysis cost appears at the disambiguating word after the ambiguity, not at the initial subject, final punctuation, or uniformly. The revision is triggered by that specific word.
questions.hint: The disambiguating word triggers revision

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Two Groups Judging Word Meaning, and What the Difference Shows
questions.learningObjective: Design a study testing group differences in semantic judgment
questions.stem: A software team's ticket asks for a design testing whether two groups differ in semantic judgment speed

answer.exemplar: Match groups on confounds, use the same word pairs in both groups, include category and rhyme conditions, and test the group by condition interaction on reaction time and accuracy

questions.explanation: Matching confounds, using identical word pairs, and including category and rhyme conditions with a group by condition interaction test directly assesses where any group difference occurs. Reaction time and accuracy capture the full profile.
questions.hint: Test the group by condition interaction

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: A Sentence That Is Slow Because of One Structural Choice
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a reading-time increase from a structural choice

stimulus.body: A ticketed reading study shows that inserting a long relative clause between subject and verb increases reading time by 180 ms, while inserting the same clause at the end of the sentence increases time by only 40 ms.

questions.stem: A software team's ticket shows 180 ms cost mid-sentence versus 40 ms at the end

options.text: Position does not matter; only clause length matters
End placement is always harder than mid placement
Mid-sentence placement disrupts the subject-verb dependency
The 40 ms end cost is a measurement error

questions.explanation: The larger cost for mid-sentence placement reflects disruption of the subject-verb dependency. Position matters beyond length, and the end-placement cost is a real, smaller effect.
questions.hint: Mid-placement breaks the dependency

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Why a Rare Word Is Slow Even When It Is Predictable
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise frequency and predictability into a lexical account
questions.stem: A software team's ticket synthesises findings that rare words stay slow even when predictable; propose an account

answer.exemplar: Frequency affects the baseline activation level of a lexical entry, while predictability provides top-down support; because these are separate mechanisms, predictability reduces but does not eliminate the frequency disadvantage

questions.explanation: Frequency sets baseline activation of a lexical entry, while predictability provides top-down support. Because they are separate mechanisms, predictability reduces but does not eliminate the frequency disadvantage.
questions.hint: Separate baseline activation from top-down support

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: A Picture That Has Been Named Before It Is Shown
questions.learningObjective: Compute the naming benefit ratio from priming data
questions.stem: A software team's ticket gives primed naming 480 ms and unprimed 600 ms; what is the benefit ratio
questions.explanation: The benefit ratio is (600 minus 480) divided by 600, which equals 0.2. The prime reduces naming time by one fifth.
questions.hint: Divide the benefit by unprimed time

questions.topic: Language: Two Word Kinds, Two Interference Effects
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise semantic and phonological effects into one framework
questions.stem: A software team's ticket synthesises semantic interference and phonological facilitation; propose a unified framework

answer.exemplar: Both effects reflect competitive activation during lexical selection: semantic competitors raise selection cost while phonological overlap boosts candidate activation, so one competitive-activation framework with task weights explains both

questions.explanation: Both effects reflect competitive activation during lexical selection: semantic competitors raise selection cost while phonological overlap boosts candidate activation. One framework with task weights explains both.
questions.hint: Unify under competitive activation

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: A Damaged Area and the Loss It Produces
questions.learningObjective: Identify the area associated with non-fluent aphasia
questions.stem: A software team's ticket asks which area's damage produces non-fluent agrammatic speech

options.text: Left superior temporal gyrus
Occipital cortex
Right inferior frontal gyrus
Left inferior frontal gyrus

questions.explanation: Damage to the left inferior frontal gyrus produces non-fluent agrammatic speech. The left superior temporal gyrus supports comprehension, and the right hemisphere and occipital cortex are not the language production site.
questions.hint: Non-fluent production is frontal left

questions.stem: A software team's ticket asks for a design measuring comprehension independently of production in fluent aphasia

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: A Failure of Repetition That Locates the Problem
questions.learningObjective: Identify the tract whose damage impairs repetition
questions.stem: A software team's ticket asks which tract's damage impairs repetition while sparing comprehension and production

options.text: Arcuate fasciculus
Corpus callosum
options.misconception: interhemispheric tract not the language link

options.text: Optic radiations
Corticospinal tract
options.misconception: motor pathway not the language link

questions.explanation: Damage to the arcuate fasciculus impairs repetition while sparing comprehension and production. The corpus callosum, optic radiations, and corticospinal tract serve other functions.
questions.hint: The tract connects comprehension and production areas

questions.stem: A software team's ticket gives 12 TOT states in 200 naming trials; what is the rate
